cards.title: Need for Speed Underground 2 online in the browser

depth.text: someone brought **Need for Speed Underground 2** into the browser so friends can **race online**

The fan project **recompiles the PC game's own code** for Chrome and Firefox, with **up to 120 fps** in widescreen, free roam, online races, and support for controllers, wheels, and touch controls. It is based on **NFSU2Recomp**, and says it is not affiliated with or endorsed by Electronic Arts.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters call hosting the game's copyrighted content legally dubious or illegal; others hope it stays up, with one arguing copyright should be 10 years.

comments.text: I played this when it was new, taking turns at the keyboard of my friend’s gaming PC. Kind of wild to revisit on my phone today and have it work perfectly. I wish the circumstances around abandonware games weren’t so tenuous, there’s so much great stuff out there and reverse engineering with AI unlocks all sorts of cool possibilities. The multiplayer features here have me thinking about other old…

The only downside is that this website isn't legal and now that it's popular it's probably getting a takedown soon. It's absolute chaos, and 2006 year old me is having so much fun. Any retail version of this game is mostly unplayable on modern PCs. Really appreciate the nostalgia bomb. I wasted so many hours of my life on this game on the original xbox.

The Doors/Snoop Dogg "Riders on the Storm" really takes me back. There are some games from that mid-2000s era that really imprinted themselves on my brain, and apparently this is one of them.

cards.title: Running a law firm on Free software

The author uses Debian, LibreOffice and Firefox, and **self-hosts almost everything** except Signal. They switched from Nextcloud to **Syncthing and radicale**, and shut down **Jitsi** because they mostly join other people's Teams or Zoom meetings.

cards.camps: Two camps: some find the setup inspiring; others worry it takes too much time to maintain and distracts from law work.

comments.text: I'm jealous, I'd love to be able to do this. I am a small cog in a big legal machine so I am stuck with whatever tech stack my firm mandates. cards.title: Pangram Image 1.0

depth.text: Pangram's new **image detector** can highlight **AI-made parts** inside an otherwise real photo

Pangram says its model got **99.96% accuracy** on **1,200 synthetic images** made from 100 real photos and 12 AI image generators. Its Flash model scored **98.7%** on DF26, a 29-point leap over the next best detector.
data: real photos used in image test

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say it works surprisingly well in tests; others say it can be fooled or could feed an arms race with generators.

comments.text: An ill advised undertaking IMO: Any attempt to build AI generated content detection systems is flawed, since the outputs of such a system may be used to train an even better fake data generator. This leads to an equilibrium state of digital uncertainty: nothing in the digital realm can be deemed as real anymore - only as digital.

At least on gemini generated images vs real ones, it works surprisingly well. Taking a photo of an AI generated image on my grubby laptop screen with my phone, moire and all, still got detected. So the signal it's using is pretty robust.

Interesting, it detected NovelAI stuff now. Looks like one can easily defeat it by having pixel-level modifications to make AI images to have characteristics of digital brush strokes and reducing "noise" in output. At least in my case for anime stuff.

From my test it works surprisingly well. I have a digital painting that is only posted very recently (therefore not in the training set). I asked GPT, Gemini and Riverflow to generate images in the same style, and use SD to add noises to remove SynthID. Pangram gave correct results for all of them (the original one is No AI; all the others are Likely AI).

There are different incentives for AI detection with text vs. images. AI detection on text is just about who gets credit for something and how much, not about the inherent value of the text itself, because the mere existence of a piece of text is never taken as proof of anything. Images are often used as proof, and so there's much more of an incentive for users of AI image generation to engage in…

cards.title: GitHub's new Git storage architecture

depth.text: GitHub built new storage so **thousands of agents** can push to **one repository** at once

In internal tests, it handled **5,000 concurrent agents** and **7,200 pushes per second** on one repository. Git objects live in Azure Blob Storage, while references go in **Ref-CAS**, a separate replicated log service; virtual replicas serve requests while dedicated compaction nodes merge packs.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see this as preparation for agent-driven repository traffic; others question whether thousands of pushes per second are a good idea or whether the design addresses current outages.

comments.text: Most of this is similar to what https://enroute.sh already did scaling Git. https://enroute.sh/blog/everyone-is-doing-git-on-s3-wrong

cards.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research

depth.text: someone says AI is **speeding up Anthropic's research** and could make progress **compound even faster**

A public METR report found Anthropic's capabilities progress went **about twice as fast** from October 2025 to October 2026, and staff self-reported a **~12x uplift** from internal models. Most of the report's most informative evidence was **redacted**; the writer says smooth compounding could imply extreme superintelligence within a year, but calls it a **naive extrapolation**.

cards.camps: Two camps: the author warns compounding could bring extreme superintelligence and severe risks; skeptical commenters say faster AI research doesn't establish that, pointing to benchmark limits, compute bottlenecks, physical testing, and human choices.

comments.text: As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests. Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on. The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on…

cards.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2

depth.text: someone broke out of a **Firecracker virtual machine** and made its host run code as **root**

They traced a **guest memory page** back to the host process, then changed the live vCPU thread’s **saved registers** so Firecracker called its write wrapper when it returned from KVM. A **serial-port write** triggered the call; this test had no jailer, while production containment can drop privileges and restrict Firecracker through namespaces and seccomp.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says the write-up is informative; another calls it “pure LLM slop.”

comments.text: I really wish they would have expanded on this paragraph in their article further: > The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM. If I'm…

I am more convinced by the day that the Nova Microhypervisor approach is correct. Do virtualization with a tiny formally verified microkernel and have complex kernels like Linux run underneath instead of letting a huge, complex, and brittle linux kernel and vm ecosystem control the hypervisor layer. https://hypervisor.org/

I have a demo service that entirely relies on Firecracker VMs: ClickBench playground, https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/playground/ It hosts hundreds of database engines - many of them have vulnerabilities, and some of them, like Pandas, are basically open RCEs regardless. We can PoC the Firecracker VM Escape on that service.

This is not a new vulnerability, it's just a description of how to exploit the PwnEscape vulnerability in practice on firecracker VMs (disclosed multiple weeks ago and discussed in some less upvoted posts on HN)

cards.title: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP

depth.text: **sodium-ion batteries** are nearing **cell-cost parity with LFP** and could mean **lower lifetime costs**

Wood Mackenzie says supply agreements already top **70 GWh**. Manufacturers could reach cell-level cost parity by late 2026, while module and system parity may wait until after 2030. It estimates **21% lower total cost of ownership** over 20 years, though the global average sodium-ion battery cost is $229/kWh, versus approximately $200/kWh for LFP.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters want sodium-ion for home batteries and praise its safety; others say mere cost parity is disappointing or question the article's LFP price figures.

cards.title: We've built an open-source feature flag server for 11 years

depth.text: someone built an **open-source** tool for **switching features** on and off without redeploying

Unleash creator Ivar says it began as an **internal tool** in **2014**. Its server-side SDKs fetch flag config, then evaluate it inside your app, so user data stays there and a flag check is a **memory lookup**, not a network call.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say a server for booleans adds infrastructure; supporters say the service has real value for teams that want it.

glossary.recompiler: A tool that changes a program's code into a form that can run on a different system.

glossary.free roam: A game mode where you can explore and drive around without starting a race.

glossary.transformer: A kind of language model that can weigh how different words in a passage relate to each other.

glossary.parameters: Learned values inside a model that shape the answers it gives.
glossary.scaling: Making an AI model bigger or giving it more training and computing power to see whether it improves.

glossary.n-grams: A way for a keyboard to guess upcoming words using the words typed before them.

glossary.payment-skimming: Stealing someone's payment details by collecting them on what looks like a normal checkout page.
glossary.SMS: Short Message Service: text messages sent between phones.
glossary.Electron: A tool for making desktop apps with web technologies, so a web-style app can run like a regular computer program.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.GPUI: A tool for building app screens in Rust that uses the computer’s graphics chip instead of HTML.
glossary.like-for-like benchmark: A comparison that tests two things under the same conditions.
glossary.heatmap: A colored overlay that shows where AI-made content appears in an image.
glossary.synthetic mirror: An AI-made version of a real photo or video, created to look like the original.
glossary.frontier AI image generator: A newer, leading AI tool used to create images.
glossary.DF26: An academic test used to compare how well detectors spot AI videos.
glossary.honeypot: A computer set up to attract attacks so people can watch what attackers do.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.nginx: Web server software that listens for requests and sends website content back.
glossary.Shodan: A search engine people use to find devices connected to the internet.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.EXPERT flag: A switch in the installer that early M3 users had to turn on before support became generally available.
glossary.Thunderbolt: A connection standard for linking computers with peripherals and each other using a cable.
glossary.XDomain: A feature that lets two Thunderbolt computers connect directly to each other.
glossary.upstream-first: Doing changes in the main shared project first, rather than maintaining them separately and sending them in later.
glossary.GNU General Public License (GPL): GNU General Public License: a software licence that requires people who share changed versions to keep the same licence terms.
glossary.copyleft: A way of licensing code that lets people reuse it but requires shared changed copies to keep the same sharing rules.
glossary.knowledge graph: A way to organize information by showing how people, places, or things are connected.
glossary.daemon: A program that runs in the background and handles a task without being started each time.
glossary.kinship inference: A guess about which people are related, such as who might be family.
glossary.SQLite: A small database that can be stored in a single file.
glossary.TCC Full Disk Access: A macOS permission that gives an app access to files normally kept off limits.
glossary.GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation: a European law that sets rules for how organizations use people's personal information.
glossary.mainframe: A large central computer that many people can use, rather than each person having their own computer.
glossary.OOM: Out of memory: when a program runs out of the memory it has available.
glossary.DRAM fab: DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) fab: a factory that makes chips used as computer memory.
glossary.Ref-CAS: Reference Compare-and-Swap: a service that checks a branch still points where expected before recording a change.
glossary.virtual replica: A replaceable worker that handles repository requests and keeps a local cache that can be rebuilt.
glossary.compaction: Shortening an AI’s conversation history, often by turning it into a summary.
glossary.quorum: The group of checks that must get the right response for validation to pass.
glossary.pack: A bundle of Git data stored together; this system adds packs on pushes and later merges them.
glossary.vertical scale: Handling more developers or agents working in the same repository.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.toolchain: A set of tools used together to get a job done.
glossary.allowlist: A list of apps or people that are allowed to connect.
glossary.proxy: A go-between that gets information from another website on someone else's behalf.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.responsible disclosure: Privately reporting a security flaw so its maintainers have time to fix it before it is made public.
glossary.blocklist: A list of files or sources a tool should reject or remove.
glossary.WHOIS: A public lookup service for details about who registered a website name; those details can be hidden or outdated.
glossary.ABI: Application Binary Interface: the agreed rules software uses to communicate with other software.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.opaque handle: A reference you can use to work with something without seeing how it is built inside.
glossary.identity resolution: Matching records from different sources so they point to the right real person.
glossary.over-merging: Combining records from different people as if they belonged to one person.
glossary.confidence calibration: How well a model’s confidence scores match how often it is actually right.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.hybrid model: A setup that uses one model first and sends selected cases to another for review.
glossary.MS-DOS: Microsoft Disk Operating System: older computer software that runs programs using typed commands.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.S-1: A filing that gives investors details about a company's finances and share offering before an IPO.
glossary.lockup schedule: A timetable showing when certain shareholders are allowed to sell their shares.
glossary.Dutch auction: A way to set a sale price from buyers’ bids instead of choosing one fixed price first.
glossary.LPs: Limited partners: investors who put money into a fund run by someone else.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.commoditized: When something becomes easy to swap for similar options, so sellers struggle to stand out.
glossary.capabilities progress: How quickly AI systems get better at the abilities being measured.
glossary.compute multiplier: An improvement that lets the same amount of computer power get more AI progress.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.alignment: The effort to keep an AI's actions in line with what people want.
glossary.compounding acceleration: When each improvement helps bring about further improvements, making progress speed up again.
glossary.bare-metal programming: Writing software for a computer to run without a normal operating system in between.
glossary.UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the built-in startup software that checks a computer and starts its main software.
glossary.linking: Joining compiled pieces of a program so they can run together.
glossary.EFI system partition: A section of a disk where a computer keeps files it needs to start up.
glossary.external symbols: Names of functions that a program expects to find in other code.
glossary.bootloader: A small program that starts a computer and loads its main software.
glossary.microVM: A small, separate computer environment for running a job; here, it gets thrown away when the job ends.
glossary.vCPU: Virtual CPU: a processor assigned to a virtual machine.
glossary.KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux feature for running virtual machines.
glossary.EPT: Extended Page Tables: tables that translate a virtual machine’s memory addresses into locations in the host machine’s memory.
glossary.pt_regs: A record of the CPU’s saved state, including where a program should resume.
glossary.ASLR: Address Space Layout Randomization: a way to move parts of a program around each time it runs, making some attacks harder.
glossary.jailer: A helper that starts Firecracker with limits on its permissions and access.
glossary.namespaces: A Linux feature that gives a process its own view of things like other processes or the network.
glossary.seccomp: A Linux control that limits which requests a program can make to the system’s core.
glossary.root: The highest level of control on a computer, with permission to change system settings and files.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.proposed repo: A place Ubuntu puts updates for testing before moving them into the regular updates.
glossary.QA: Quality assurance: checking that software works as expected before people rely on it.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.mitigation: A step taken to make a problem less harmful or disruptive.
glossary.sodium-ion battery: A battery that uses sodium rather than lithium; this article discusses it for storing electricity.
glossary.LFP: Lithium iron phosphate: a type of rechargeable battery used here as a comparison for sodium-ion batteries.
glossary.cell-level cost parity: When the battery cells themselves cost about the same, before comparing the rest of a complete storage system.
glossary.GWh: Gigawatt-hours: a measure of an amount of electricity, often used to describe how much a battery can store.
glossary.total cost of ownership: The full cost of using something over its lifetime, not just what it costs to buy.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.headless: Software that another program can control without a person using its regular screen.
glossary.element tree: A nested outline of the parts that make up a screen, such as a label inside a window.
glossary.native UI: An app’s screens and controls built for a device’s own system.
glossary.feature flag: A switch developers can use to turn a feature on or off without removing it from the program.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.local evaluation: Checking a flag inside the application, rather than making a network call each time.
glossary.microplastics: Tiny pieces of plastic that can shed from products and end up in food or the environment.
glossary.compostable: Able to break down into material that can be used as compost.
glossary.brew path: The parts inside a coffee machine that hot water and coffee pass through.
